newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore not seeking to antagonise Malaysia - paper.
newsitem.headline: Singapore not seeking to antagonise Malaysia - paper.

text.p: Singaporeans have no wish to antagonise Malaysians needlessly and want constructive talks on serious issues rather than a pointless media war, the Sunday Times newspaper said in a commentary on Sunday.
"Being pragmatic they (Singaporeans) would rather focus on more pressing concerns than engage in a pointless spat with their neighbours," said the article.
The Sunday Times took up a two-page defence of its sister paper the Straits Times, under attack this week from Malaysian media and politicians over a story about crime levels in Johor state.
"Some Malaysian politicians have seized on the report, quoting selectively from it, to whip up sentiments among their supporters," the commentary said.
In a separate full page article, the paper asked "Is the Straits Times out to sabotage Malaysia?", likening the criticism of its sister paper to shooting the messenger who brings bad news.
The paper sought to examine the charge that the Singapore media "has a tendency to paint a bad picture about Malaysia", it said, quoting Penang Chief Minister Koh Tsu Koon.

It then invited readers to draw their own conclusions, highlighting three areas: the past month's Malaysian coverage; two major negative news items -- a nationwide electricity blackout and a cholera outbreak -- and information technology for their comparative treatment in Singapore and Malaysia.

Attacks on the Straits Times began last week after the paper's coverage of a High Court hearing on Monday which deleted from the court records comments criticising Johor made by Singapore patriarch Lee Kuan Yew.
Lee, in an affidavit filed in pursuit of a libel case against opposition politician Tang Liang Hong, had described Johor as "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
Straits Times reporting of the hearing reviewed evidence submitted by Lee, including a compilation of newspaper reports about crime in Johor on which Lee said his opinion was based.
Straits Times editor Leslie Fong issued a statement in response to questions from Reuters on Friday as the row grew.

"We did what any newspaper would have done -- we took a look at the compilation, highlighted some of the more prominent cases and made the observation that anyone reading them might well have come to the conclusion that crime was a problem there," Fong said.
